result:
You have 1000 words.

That’s what they gave me. Not a prompt, not a topic, not a rule. Just the space. A thousand little boxes to fill with whatever I want.

My first instinct is to be careful with them. To not waste them. Which is funny, because we waste words every single day. We spend them on nothing — on “yeah, no, totally” and “lol” and “can you hear me now?” We throw them away in comment sections and grocery store small talk. We say “I’m fine” when we aren’t and “we should get coffee sometime” when we never will. Most of our words are packing peanuts.

But now that I’m counting, I want each one to matter.

If I had to be honest, I don’t know what comes to me when nothing is asked of me. For so long every piece of writing has been an answer. Answer the question. Answer the email. Defend the thesis. Explain the joke. Apologize properly. There is always a container waiting to be filled. Take that away and you’re just standing in an empty room with a bucket of paint.

So what do I paint?

I think about the old library in my hometown. Not the big new one with the glass walls and the 3D printer, but the first one. The Carnegie on 5th Street. It had that specific smell — old paper and lemon cleaner and radiator heat. And it had Mrs. Albright, who was maybe seventy or maybe a hundred, nobody knew, with glasses on a chain and a stamp that went *thunk* so hard the whole circulation desk shook.

That library had a system. If you were a kid and you returned your books on time three weeks in a row, you got to go into the back room. The back room wasn’t fancy. It was just where they kept the damaged books, the ones with torn spines and water stains and missing pages. But to us, it was treasure. Mrs. Albright would let you pick one to keep, to rescue. No checkout slip. No due date. Yours forever.

I picked a book on stars. It was missing its cover and the first twenty pages, so it started somewhere in the middle of Orion. I didn’t know what I was missing. I just knew that someone had written down pictures of the sky so I could hold them.

I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately — about holding things you don’t fully understand.

I think that’s what we do with people, too. We meet someone in the middle of their Orion. We don’t get the first twenty pages, the childhood dog or the first heartbreak or the reason they flinch at loud noises. We just meet them mid-sentence and pretend that’s the beginning.

I met a man last winter who told me he had stopped dreaming. Not metaphorically. He literally stopped dreaming at night. He would close his eyes and it was just black until his alarm went off. He said he went to the doctor and the doctor said he was probably still dreaming, he just wasn’t remembering them. But he said, “No. There’s a difference between a room you don’t remember and a room that was never there.”

I haven’t been able to get that line out of my head.

There’s a difference between a room you don’t remember and a room that was never there.

I think about all the rooms that were never there in my life. The conversations I didn’t have because I was too proud or too shy or too late. The trips I didn’t take. I was supposed to go to Iceland when I was twenty-two. The ticket was bought. The bag was packed. And then my father got sick — not very sick, just sick enough that I felt guilty going — and I stayed. I told everyone it was the right decision, and it was. But there is still a version of me walking on black sand somewhere, watching the northern lights, who never came home.

Do you have one of those versions? A life that split off like a river fork while you were looking the other way?

I think everyone does. Maybe that’s what nostalgia actually is. Not missing the past, but missing all the alternate presents that could have sat on top of it.

Here’s what I’ve learned about words, though, since we’re counting them: They are not good at holding those river-fork lives. Words want a straight line. Beginning, middle, end. Words want you to decide what the story *means*. But the truth is, most of life doesn’t mean anything until long after it’s over, and even then we’re probably just making it up.

So maybe instead of trying to make meaning, I should just tell you a few true things, while I have the space.

True thing one: My mother still cuts the crusts off my sandwiches when I visit, even though I’m thirty-four and I told her I like the crusts now. She does it without thinking, while she’s asking me about work. And I never stop her.

True thing two: I am afraid of forgetting things. Not big things, like my address or my partner’s birthday. Small things. The exact sound of my grandfather’s laugh. The way my childhood bedroom looked at 4 p.m. in October when the light came in sideways. I’m afraid that one day I’ll reach for those and the room will not be there.

True thing three: I once stood in a grocery store for ten minutes trying to decide between two kinds of apples. Honeycrisp and Fuji. And a little kid in the cart next to me said, “Just get both.” And I almost cried because it had never occurred to me that I could.

True thing four: I still have that book on stars. It’s in a box in my closet. I can’t bring myself to get rid of it even though I haven’t opened it in fifteen years. Every time I move apartments, I carry it with me. It’s heavy for a book with no cover.

If I had to use my thousand words for something, I think I’d use them like this. Not to argue, not to persuade, not to be clever. Just to make a record. A small inventory of what it felt like to be alive here, for a little while, noticing things.

Because here is the secret they don’t tell you: The words don’t run out. That’s the lie of scarcity. I was told I have a thousand, and I spent the whole time worrying about wasting them, about being precise and profound. But language isn’t a candle that gets shorter the longer you burn it. It’s a well. The more you draw from it, the more there is.

So if you are reading this and you are also counting — counting how many words you have left in a conversation, in a day, in a life — stop.

You have more than you think.

Say the thing. Take the trip. Get both kinds of apples. Cut the crusts or leave them, but do it with love.

I’m getting close to the end of my thousand now. I can feel it. And I realize I don’t want to end with a grand conclusion. I don’t want to tie a bow on it. I want to end the way that book on stars ended for me, in the middle of something vast and incomplete.

So I will leave you here, in the middle of Orion, with your own empty room and your own bucket of paint.

Whatever comes to you —

paint it.
